69699.etyen:
The lowercase form of Z, from Latin Z. The Latin letter was reintroduced from Ancient Greek Ζ (Z, “zeta”), itself derived from Phoenician 𐤆 (z, “zayin; weapon”). It was placed at the end of the Latin alphabet when it was reintroduced for Greek names and loanwords. / Derived from Latin Z, ultimately from Ancient Greek Ζ (Z), from Phoenician 𐤆 (zayin, “weapon”), with the early alphabetic form transmitted through Etruscan.
The letter occurred in the archaic Latin alphabet, where it originally occupied the position after ⟨F⟩. After the sound represented by the letter disappeared from native Latin, ⟨Z⟩ fell out of ordinary use. It was reintroduced under Augustus for writing Greek loanwords and was placed at the end of the Latin alphabet. Norwegian inherited the letter through the Latin alphabet and the Danish–Norwegian written tradition.

28483.etyen:
Compound of kamuflasje (“camouflage”) + drakt (“suit, outfit”), literally “camouflage suit”.
The first element kamuflasje (“camouflage”) derives from French camouflage (“camouflage”), a verbal noun of camoufler (“to disguise, camouflage”); the further origin of the French verb is disputed.
The second element drakt (“suit, outfit; animal coat or plumage”) derives from Middle Low German dracht (“what is carried; clothing”), from Proto-Germanic *drahtuz (“pulling, carrying”), itself derived from *draganą (“to draw, pull, carry”); the further origin of the verb is uncertain.
Compare Norwegian Nyno

116803.etyen:
Borrowed from English evangelical (“evangelical”). The English source is evangelic (“evangelic”) + -al (“adjective-forming suffix”); evangelic is from Old French evangelique (“evangelic, evangelical”), from Latin evangelicus (“evangelical”), itself based on evangelium (“gospel”), ultimately from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news; gospel”).
The first element of εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion) is related to εὐ- (eu-, “good, well”), from Proto-Hellenic *ehu- (“good”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁su- (“good”). The further origin of the Proto-Indo-European combining form is uncertain.

1000515.etyen:
Unadapted borrowing from French Nancy, the name of a city in northeastern France. The French place name continues Late Latin Nanciaco, also attested as Nanciacum and Nanceiacum, probably from Gaulish *Nantiākom (“domain of Nantios”).
The Gaulish place name is generally analysed as containing the personal name Nantios and the locative suffix *-ākom. The personal name may itself derive from Proto-Celtic *nantos (“stream, river; valley”).
Compare German Nanzig and Luxembourgish Nanzeg, continuations of the same historical place name.

1000771.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse *Álasund, from áll (“eel”) or áll (“stripe; channel”) and sund (“sound, strait”). The name originally referred to the sound between Aspøya and Nørvøya, around which the town developed. By surface analysis, ål (“eel; stripe, channel”) + sund (“sound, strait”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Ålesund, Faroese Álasund and Icelandic Álasund.

1001027.etyen:
Origin uncertain. Probably cognate with Swedish Swedish ag (“sedge, especially great fen-sedge”). The plant name has been connected with an Indo-European root meaning “sharp, pointed”, perhaps in reference to the sharply toothed leaves of great fen-sedge, but this connection is uncertain.
If the proposed root connection is correct, compare Latin acus (“needle, point”) and ācer (“sharp”), as well as Norwegian agg (“edge; resentment”) and abbor (“perch”), which have also been connected with the same root.

1005123.etyen:
PIE word

Compound of E-dur (“E major”) + akkord (“chord”), literally “E-major chord”.
The first element E-dur (“E major”) contains the musical note name E (“E”) and dur (“major”). The adjective is from Latin dūrus (“hard”), from Proto-Italic *dūros (“hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *dweh₂rós (“long, far”), from the root *dweh₂- (“far, long”).
